events.before: Home Newsroom Notice on the Upcoming EU Tax Reform Effective July 2026 Notice on the Upcoming EU Tax Reform Effective July 2026 Press Release Jun 27, 2026 Table of Contents Policy Overview: Elimination of Duty Exemptions Different sets of rules will apply to B2C and B2B shipments Managing "Duty & Tax Disbursement Fees" from Carriers Consolidation Advice for B2C Shipments An official advisory has been issued for customers across the European Union regarding the upcoming EU Tax Reform . Effective July 1, 2026 , this major regulatory shift implemented by the European Union will impact import and customs procedures for low-value shipments entering EU member states. To ensure uninterrupted service and minimize clearance delays, all EU-based clients are urged to familiarize themselves with these new regulations. Policy Overview: Elimination of Duty Exemptions Starting July 1, 2026, the European Union will completely eliminate the customs duty exemption for low-value goods . Every single shipment bound for the EU, regardless of its value, must be formally declared and is subject to customs duties. Different sets of rules will apply to B2C and B2B shipments The EUCR introduces distinct compliance frameworks based on the nature of the recipient: 1. For B2C shipments : Goods value ≤ €150 : A flat-rate "temporary customs duty" of €3.00 per line item will be applied. For example, if a package contains 3 different product categories, the total temporary customs duty will be €9.00. Goods value > €150 : Standard tariff rates apply. Impact on IOSS : Under the current IOSS framework, JLCCNC can only collect and remit import VAT, but cannot manage the "temporary customs duty". Therefore, recipients will still need to pay the "temporary customs duty" upon importation if using non-DDP channels. 2. For B2B shipments : Regardless of the shipment value, all B2B packages must go through formal customs clearance and pay duties based on the actual HS code corresponding to the goods (standard applicable tariff rates), bypassing the €3.00 flat-rate rule. Managing "Duty & Tax Disbursement Fees" from Carriers When carriers like DHL, UPS, or FedEx pay customs duties and taxes upfront on behalf of the recipient, they charge a "duty & tax disbursement fee" to the party responsible for the tax. These fees vary significantly by country and carrier (such as tiered brackets or specific minimum charges per shipment). Consolidation Advice for B2C Shipments To optimize your shipping costs under the new EU regulations, we highly recommend consolidating your orders. For B2C customers, if you combine multiple items or orders into a single shipment to bring the total goods value above €150 , the shipment will become eligible for standard tariff rates instead of the €3.00 flat-rate temporary customs duty per line item. For many multi-item orders, utilizing standard tariffs through consolidation can be significantly more cost-effective. For more information regarding specific handling fees, tax calculations, and country-by-country Duty & Tax Disbursement Fee, please read our full EU Customs Reform (EUCR) July 2026 – Client FAQ . events.before: Home Newsroom JLC Technology Group Launches USDC Payments for Faster, Lower-Fee Checkout JLC Technology Group Launches USDC Payments for Faster, Lower-Fee Checkout Press Release Aug 27, 2026 Table of Contents Faster and Lower-Cost Payments with USDC USDC Payment Availability How to Pay with USDC USDC Payment FAQs Supporting a More Flexible Digital Manufacturing Experience About JLC Technology Group About JLCCNC We are thrilled to announce that JLC Technology Group now officially accepts stablecoin payments . US-based customers can now pay for JLCCNC, JLC3DP, JLCPCB, and JLCMC orders using USDC—enabling near-instant settlement, lower transaction fees, and 24/7 availability. Faster and Lower-Cost Payments with USDC Paying with stablecoins brings several tangible advantages directly to customers: Lower transaction costs – Customers only pay the blockchain network fee (Gas fee), which is typically a fraction of a dollar on networks like Solana or Polygon. There are no cross-border surcharges or hidden bank fees. No bank account or credit card required – Customers only need a crypto wallet, such as MetaMask or Coinbase Wallet. Fast and straightforward checkout – Customers can select stablecoin at checkout, connect their wallet, and confirm the transaction in just a few clicks, without entering lengthy card details or bank information. In short, USDC payments provide lower fees, instant processing, and a smoother checkout experience. USDC Payment Availability The current stablecoin payment setup includes the following conditions: Item Current Rule Supported business JLCPCB, JLC3DP, JLCCNC, and JLCMC Supported region United States only Supported stablecoin USDC only Supported networks Tempo, Ethereum, Solana, Polygon, Base Maximum per transaction Up to 10,000 USD Refund options Original wallet or JLC balance These rules reflect JLC's current stablecoin payment setup. Customers outside the United States will not see the USDC payment option at this stage. Any future expansion of supported regions will be announced separately. This launch supports USDC only . Other stablecoins, including USDP and USDG, are not currently supported. How to Pay with USDC Paying with stablecoins is simple and requires four steps. Step 1: Select Payment Method at Checkout On the JLC order confirmation page, select "Crypto (USDC)" . Step 2: Connect Your Crypto Wallet Customers will be redirected to a secure payment page, where they can connect using MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet , or any WalletConnect-compatible wallet. Step 3: Confirm and Sign the Transaction The payment page displays the amount due, denominated in USDC and pegged 1:1 to USD. Customers can confirm and sign the transaction in their wallet. Step 4: Payment Complete Once the transaction is confirmed on-chain, the order status will update automatically. Funds are settled in USD to JLC's account — JLC does not hold or manage any cryptocurrency. USDC Payment FAQs Q1: Which stablecoins are currently supported? USDC only. Other stablecoins, including USDT, USDP, and USDG, are not currently supported. Q2: Are there fees for stablecoin payments? Customers are responsible for the Gas fees (network transaction fees) of the chosen blockchain network. Fees vary by network — Solana, Polygon, and Base offer extremely low fees, often just a few cents. JLC Technology Group does not charge any additional fees for stablecoin payments. Q3: Is there a transaction limit? The per-transaction limit is 10,000 USD. Orders exceeding this amount are not eligible for stablecoin payment and require an alternative payment method. Q4: Are refunds supported? Yes. Refunds are processed back to the customer's original wallet or to the customer's JLC balance, subject to customer setup. Q5: Which regions are supported? Currently, stablecoin payments are available only for customers in the United States. Other countries are not supported at this time. Q6: How long does a stablecoin payment take to confirm? Confirmation time varies by network. Ethereum typically takes 3–15 minutes, while Solana, Polygon, and Base usually confirm within 5–30 seconds. During network congestion, times may be longer. Customers are recommended to use faster networks like Solana or Polygon for the quickest experience. Supporting a More Flexible Digital Manufacturing Experience The launch of USDC payments provides US-based customers with another way to complete orders across JLC Technology Group's digital manufacturing ecosystem. By supporting stablecoin payments, JLCCNC and other JLC platforms provide customers with a payment option designed around faster processing, lower transaction costs, and 24/7 availability. About JLC Technology Group Founded in 2006, JLC Technology Group provides integrated electronics and mechanical manufacturing services to more than 9.5 million customers across over 180 countries and regions. Its ecosystem includes EasyEDA for PCB design, JLCPCB for PCB fabrication and assembly, JLC3DP for additive manufacturing, JLCCNC for CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication, and JLCMC for mechanical components—enabling customers to move from prototype to production through a full-stack digital manufacturing platform. About JLCCNC JLCCNC is an online manufacturing platform providing professional CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication services for engineers, product developers, businesses, and makers worldwide. With a range of manufacturing capabilities and materials, JLCCNC helps customers accelerate prototyping and production with quality, speed, and affordability. As part of JLC Technology Group , JLCCNC provides customers with access to the group's integrated digital manufacturing ecosystem, including electronics manufacturing, 3D printing, and mechanical components. USDC Payment Availability The current stablecoin payment setup includes the following conditions: Item Current Rule Supported business JLCPCB, JLC3DP, JLCCNC, and JLCMC Supported region United States only Supported stablecoin USDC only Supported networks Tempo, Ethereum, Solana, Polygon, Base Maximum per transaction Up to 10,000 USD Refund options Original wallet or JLC balance These rules reflect JLC's current stablecoin payment setup. Customers outside the United States will not see the USDC payment option at this stage. Any future expansion of supported regions will be announced separately. This launch supports USDC only . Other stablecoins, including USDP and USDG, are not currently supported. How to Pay with USDC Paying with stablecoins is simple and requires four steps. Step 1: Select Payment Method at Checkout On the JLC order confirmation page, select "Crypto (USDC)" . Step 2: Connect Your Crypto Wallet Customers will be redirected to a secure payment page, where they can connect using MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet , or any WalletConnect-compatible wallet. Step 3: Confirm and Sign the Transaction The payment page displays the amount due, denominated in USDC and pegged 1:1 to USD. Customers can confirm and sign the transaction in their wallet. Step 4: Payment Complete Once the transaction is confirmed on-chain, the order status will update automatically. Funds are settled in USD to JLC's account — JLC does not hold or manage any cryptocurrency. USDC Payment FAQs Q1: Which stablecoins are currently supported? USDC only. Other stablecoins, including USDT, USDP, and USDG, are not currently supported. Q2: Are there fees for stablecoin payments? Customers are responsible for the Gas fees (network transaction fees) of the chosen blockchain network. Fees vary by network — Solana, Polygon, and Base offer extremely low fees, often just a few cents. JLC Technology Group does not charge any additional fees for stablecoin payments. Q3: Is there a transaction limit? The per-transaction limit is 10,000 USD. Orders exceeding this amount are not eligible for stablecoin payment and require an alternative payment method. Q4: Are refunds supported? Yes. Refunds are processed back to the customer's original wallet or to the customer's JLC balance, subject to customer setup. Q5: Which regions are supported? Currently, stablecoin payments are available only for customers in the United States. Other countries are not supported at this time. Q6: How long does a stablecoin payment take to confirm? Confirmation time varies by network. Ethereum typically takes 3–15 minutes, while Solana, Polygon, and Base usually confirm within 5–30 seconds. During network congestion, times may be longer. Customers are recommended to use faster networks like Solana or Polygon for the quickest experience. Supporting a More Flexible Digital Manufacturing Experience The launch of USDC payments provides US-based customers with another way to complete orders across JLC Technology Group's digital manufacturing ecosystem. By supporting stablecoin payments, JLCCNC and other JLC platforms provide customers with a payment option designed around faster processing, lower transaction costs, and 24/7 availability. About JLC Technology Group Founded in 2006, JLC Technology Group provides integrated electronics and mechanical manufacturing services to more than 9.5 million customers across over 180 countries and regions. Its ecosystem includes EasyEDA for PCB design, JLCPCB for PCB fabrication and assembly, JLC3DP for additive manufacturing, JLCCNC for CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication, and JLCMC for mechanical components—enabling customers to move from prototype to production through a full-stack digital manufacturing platform. About JLCCNC JLCCNC is an online manufacturing platform providing professional CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication services for engineers, product developers, businesses, and makers worldwide. With a range of manufacturing capabilities and materials, JLCCNC helps customers accelerate prototyping and production with quality, speed, and affordability. As part of JLC Technology Group , JLCCNC provides customers with access to the group's integrated digital manufacturing ecosystem, including electronics manufacturing, 3D printing, and mechanical components. events.before: Home Newsroom JLC Digital Manufacturing Achieves PCI DSS v4.0.1 Level 1 Certification JLC Digital Manufacturing Achieves PCI DSS v4.0.1 Level 1 Certification Press Release Jul 24, 2026 Table of Contents Strengthening Payment Security for Global Customers Secure Payment Infrastructure Supporting Secure Digital Manufacturing About JLC Digital Manufacturing JLC Digital Manufacturing has achieved Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) v4.0.1 Level 1 certification , the highest level of PCI DSS compliance. The certification covers the company's major overseas business platforms, including JLCCNC, JLCPCB, JLC3DP, and JLCMC , reinforcing payment security and data protection for customers worldwide. The certification was independently assessed by atsec information security , a Qualified Security Assessor (QSA). This achievement builds upon JLC Digital Manufacturing's previously obtained ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Information Security Management System and ISO/IEC 27701:2019 Privacy Information Management System certifications, further strengthening the company's information security governance framework and its commitment to secure cross-border digital services. Strengthening Payment Security for Global Customers PCI DSS is the internationally recognized security standard established by major international payment card brands, including Visa and MasterCard, to protect payment card information. Version 4.0.1 establishes comprehensive security requirements covering areas such as network protection, encryption, access control, vulnerability management, security monitoring, and governance. By achieving PCI DSS v4.0.1 Level 1 certification, JLC Digital Manufacturing demonstrates that its payment security controls have been independently assessed against internationally recognized industry standards. For customers, this certification provides additional confidence that payment information is protected according to globally accepted security requirements throughout the online transaction process. Secure Payment Infrastructure JLC Digital Manufacturing protects online payments through industry-standard encryption, secure tokenization technologies, and trusted payment service providers, including Stripe and PayPal. The company's payment architecture is designed to protect cardholder information during transmission while reducing the handling of sensitive payment data within its own systems. In accordance with PCI DSS requirements, JLC Digital Manufacturing does not store unencrypted cardholder data, helping minimize potential security risks. These security measures support the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of payment information for customers conducting business through the company's global digital platforms. Supporting Secure Digital Manufacturing As AI technologies and intelligent manufacturing continue to accelerate the evolution of the electronics industry, cybersecurity and payment security have become increasingly important across global supply chains. For JLC Digital Manufacturing, protecting customer information and enabling secure online transactions are fundamental to delivering reliable digital manufacturing services. With internationally recognized certifications including ISO/IEC 27001 , ISO/IEC 27701 , and PCI DSS v4.0.1 Level 1 , JLC Digital Manufacturing will continue enhancing its security capabilities while providing trusted services for engineers, innovators, and businesses worldwide. About JLC Digital Manufacturing Founded in 2006, JLC Digital Manufacturing provides integrated electronics and mechanical manufacturing services to more than 9.5 million customers across over 180 countries and regions . Its ecosystem includes JLCCNC for CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication, EasyEDA for PCB design, JLCPCB for PCB fabrication, component sourcing, and PCB assembly, JLC3DP for additive manufacturing, and JLCMC for mechanical components, enabling customers to move from prototype to production through a full-stack digital manufacturing platform. For JLCCNC customers, this certification provides additional assurance that online payment information is protected according to internationally recognized security standards. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay to Exhibit at SIDO Lyon 2026: Meet Us at Booth E122 PCBWay to Exhibit at SIDO Lyon 2026: Meet Us at Booth E122 by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News As smart technologies continue to transform industrial products and connected devices, reliable hardware manufacturing has become an essential part of turning innovative concepts into real-world products. From September 16 to 17, 2026, SIDO Lyon 2026 will bring together technology providers, industrial companies, startups, and innovation professionals at the Lyon Convention Centre in France. The event focuses on the convergence of IoT, Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, and Extended Reality (XR), with a strong emphasis on practical industrial applications and digital transformation. PCBWay will be exhibiting at Booth E122. We warmly invite you to visit us and explore how our manufacturing services can support your next hardware project. PCBWay at SIDO Lyon 2026 Event: SIDO Lyon 2026 Date: September 16–17, 2026 Venue: Lyon Convention Centre, Cité Internationale, Lyon, France Booth: E122 SIDO Lyon is designed to connect technology solutions with companies working on real-world digitalization and Industry 4.0 projects. The 2026 edition is expected to bring together more than 300 exhibitors, with technologies covering IoT, AI, robotics, digital twins, XR, cybersecurity, and prototyping. For hardware developers, these technologies ultimately depend on one critical foundation: reliable physical products that can move efficiently from concept to production. From Prototype to Production Developing an IoT device, robotic system, industrial controller, or smart product often involves more than designing a PCB. Hardware teams may need to coordinate electronics, mechanical components, enclosures, prototypes, and final assembly throughout the development process. PCBWay provides a range of manufacturing services to support these requirements, including: PCB Manufacturing PCB Assembly (PCBA) HDI and Flex PCB Rigid-Flex PCB CNC Machining 3D Printing Injection Molding Sheet Metal Fabrication Box Build Assembly This integrated approach helps hardware teams reduce the complexity of working with multiple manufacturing suppliers and makes it easier to move from an initial prototype toward small-batch and production manufacturing. Meet PCBWay at Booth E122 If you are attending SIDO Lyon 2026, come and visit PCBWay at Booth E122. The exhibition will be an opportunity to discuss your current or upcoming hardware projects, explore manufacturing solutions, and learn more about how PCBWay can support projects ranging from early-stage prototypes to production. Whether you are developing an IoT device, robotic system, industrial controller, smart sensor, embedded product, or other electronic hardware, our team will be happy to discuss your manufacturing requirements. Visit us at Booth E122 and let's bring your next hardware idea to life. Verify Now Blog > PCB Design Layout Guidelines for Routing PCB Design Layout Guidelines for Routing by: Mia Jul 17,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Design Guideline PCB Routing PCB Layout 1. Length Control in Routing Length controlling is very important in PCB design. The traces should be kept as short as possible to avoid introducing unnecessary interference due to excessive length. For important signal traces, such as clock signal traces, be sure to place its oscillator very close to the device. 2. Direction Control in Routing The routing directions of adjacent layers should be orthogonal to avoid the signal traces of adjacent layers running in the same direction, thus reducing unnecessary crosstalk between layers. 3. Rules for Chamfer Sharp angles and right angles should be avoided in PCB design, otherwise, unnecessary radiation will be generated and the process performance will be poor. 4. Open Loop Detection in Routing Generally, dangling lines are not allowed. This is mainly to avoid the "antenna effect" and reduce unnecessary interference radiation and reception. Otherwise, serious consequences may occur. 5. Try to Avoid Self-loop Routing When designing PCB, we should pay attention to the situation where signal traces form self-loops between different layers. Especially when routing multi-layer boards, signal traces are routed between layers, which has a greater chance of forming self-loops. Self-loops can cause radiation interference. 6. Rules for Ground Loop The minimal loop rule states that the loop area formed by a signal trace and its return path should be as small as possible. The smaller the loop area, the less external radiation it emits and the less interference it receives from the outside. 7. Rules for the Integrity of Power and Ground Layers For areas with dense vias, care should be taken to avoid the holes connecting to each other in the hollowed-out areas of the power and ground layers, which would segment the plane layer. This may destroy the integrity of the plane layer and further increase the loop area of ​​the signal trace in the ground layer. 8. 3W Rule In order to reduce crosstalk between traces, the trace spacing should be large enough. When the center-to-center distance between traces is at least three times the space width, 70% of the electric field will not interfere with each other, known as the 3W rule. To achieve 98% of the electric field not interfering with each other, a 10W spacing can be used. 9. Shielding Protection Shielding protection corresponds to the ground loop rule, which is actually to minimize the loop area of ​​the signal. It is more common in some important signals, such as clock signals and synchronization signals. For some particularly important, high-frequency signals, a coaxial cable shielding design should be considered. This involves isolating the signal traces with ground traces on all sides (top, bottom, left, and right). Additionally, careful consideration must be given to how effectively to connect the shield ground to the actual ground plane. 10. Rules for Impedance Matching Check The routing width in the same network should be kept consistent. Changes in trace width can cause non-uniform characteristic impedance of the circuit, leading to reflections when the transmission speed is high. This should be avoided in the design whenever possible. Under certain conditions, such as structures similar to lead-out traces of connectors or the lead-out traces of BGA packages, changes in trace width may be unavoidable, so the effective length of the inconsistent sections should be minimized. 11. Rules for Overlapping Power and Ground Layers Different power layers should avoid overlapping in space to reduce interference between different power supplies. This is especially important for power supplies with significantly different voltages. If it is difficult to avoid, consider placing a ground plane in between. 12. 20H Principle To prevent board edge radiation, the power plane should be retracted during design. Using H (the dielectric thickness between the power and ground) as a unit, a retraction of 20H can confine 70% of the electric field within the edge of the ground layer, while a retraction of 100H can confine 98% of the electric field within it. Verify Now Blog > HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design by: Mila Sep 03,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hdi pcb HDI pcb design optical module pcb high speed pcb layout An optical module PCB is a typical high-frequency, high-density HDI PCB precision board. Its material selection is closely related to transmission rate, link length, loss budget, and device platforms. While 10G and lower modules can use materials like high-Tg FR-4, high-speed modules operating at 25G, 56G, 100G, 400G, and 800G impose stringent requirements on low-loss materials, impedance control, and manufacturing consistency. Below are seven core layout design points and key differences compared to standard PCBs, focusing on high speed pcb layout and practical signal integrity engineering without rigid design fallacies. 1. Substrate Selection and StackUp Design Substrate selection and layer stackup form the foundation for stable high-frequency transmission, directly determining link insertion loss, impedance accuracy, and signal integrity. Multi-Dimensional Rate-Matched Selection: For 25G+ channels, select substrates considering Nyquist frequency, link length, insertion loss budget, dielectric loss, copper foil roughness, and stackup. For long-distance or low-loss channels, choose mid-to-low loss high-speed substrates. Non-critical areas like low-speed control and power can use high-Tg FR-4 to balance performance and cost on an optical module PCB. Adjacent Reference Ground Planes: High-speed differential signal layers should adopt a "signal-reference ground" structure to minimize edge-field coupling. Power layers should pair with adjacent ground layers to optimize PDN impedance via inter-layer capacitance. Pre-Simulation Impedance Modeling: Determine stackup parameters early through SI simulation. The industry standard target is typically 100 ohms differential impedance, with high-performance channels strictly controlling tolerances within +/- 5%. 2. High-Speed Differential TX/RX Signal Integrity High-speed differential signals are the core of data transmission in an optical module PCB. Design should focus on eliminating geometric discontinuities and parasitic interference. Symmetry and Equal Length: Match trace widths, spacing, bends, and via layouts for differential pairs. Advanced HDI pcb design requires controlling intra-pair length skew to prevent differential-to-common mode noise conversion. Trace Geometry Continuity: Use 45-degree angles or smooth arc transitions instead of rigid 90-degree turns. High-frequency reflections stem mostly from vias, pads, stubs, and split reference planes rather than standard trace corners. Minimal Via Structures and Stub Optimization: Minimize layer transitions. For long through-hole structures, apply back-drilling to remove residual stubs, cutting down reflections and resonances. （Backdrill + Via Stub） Unbroken High-Frequency Return Paths: Avoid routing differential traces across ground splits or slot gaps. Provide nearby stitching ground vias whenever signals switch layers. (Differential Pair + Reference Plane + Return Path) Crosstalk Mitigation: Apply the 3W rule during initial layout for proper spacing. For 112G PAM4 ultra-high-speed scenarios, refine trace spacing with 3D EM simulation and add ground via shielding walls where necessary. 3. Optoelectronic Isolation and Sensitive Layout Optical modules combine sensitive analog signals with high-speed digital logic. The analog front-end requires isolation from power and digital noise. Physical Isolation: Separate TOSA/ROSA components and TIA analog circuits from high-speed digital traces and switching power supplies based on form factors (SFP, QSFP, OSFP). Short Analog Traces: Keep weak analog traces from optical devices to TIA and driver ICs as short as possible, avoiding parallel routing alongside high-speed digital lines. Analog Circuit Shielding: Implement localized ground shielding or small metal shields around laser drivers and TIA circuits to isolate high-frequency digital noise. 4. Power Integrity (PI) Optimization Focus on low-impedance return paths, minimal current loops, and sub-region noise reduction. Minimal Loop Decoupling: Configure decoupling networks based on target PDN impedance. Place capacitors close to power pins to minimize parasitic inductance. Solid Ground Plane Priority: Maintain a continuous, low-impedance ground plane across the HDI PCB to provide a solid reference. Apply localized filtering for sensitive analog zones rather than single-point star grounding across the board. Thermal Copper Pour for Power Chips: Place large copper areas with thermal via arrays beneath heat-generating components like laser drivers to disperse heat quickly. 5. Thermal Management in HDI PCB Design Optical module DSPs, optical drivers, and laser diodes generate concentrated heat. High temperatures cause device aging, DK/Df parameter drift, and impedance shifts. Efficient Thermal Paths: Place dense thermal via arrays under high-power devices (DSP, TOSA) to transfer heat from the optical module PCB inner layers to the metal housing. Hot/Cold Component Partitioning: Isolate heat sources from temperature-sensitive optical and clock components to prevent thermal drift and premature aging. Symmetrical Design against Warpage: Balance copper distribution and layer stack-ups across the HDI PCB to manage thermal-mechanical stress during reflow soldering. （Thermal Path IC → Thermal Via → Copper Plane → Housing） 6. EMC and Grounding for High Speed PCB Layout Symmetrical Routing for Common-Mode Noise: Maintain structural symmetry in high-speed differential traces to reduce EMI radiation. Connect the module metal shell to the PCB ground for low-impedance shielding. Interface ESD Protection : Place TVS diodes and common-mode chokes near edge connectors to route ESD currents quickly to chassis ground. Isolate Interference Sources: Keep power inductors and switching regulators away from sensitive RX analog inputs to prevent magnetic coupling. 7. DFM Guidelines for Optical Module PCB Manufacturing Precise HDI pcb design and assembly standards ensure manufacturing yield for dense components. Precision Soldering Design: Use Via-in-Pad or micro-vias for high-density BGAs. For QFN thermal pads, use segmented stencil openings to reduce solder voiding and floating. Optical Alignment Tolerance: Match mechanical outline and mounting hole tolerances precisely with metal housings to avoid optical misalignments. Test Points and Gold Fingers: Keep test points off high-speed trunk lines. Use hard gold plating for edge connector gold fingers to ensure durability across insertion cycles. 8.Optical Module PCB vs Standard PCB Core Differences Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design HDI PCB Layout Guide for High Speed Optical Module PCB Design by: Mila Sep 03,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hdi pcb HDI pcb design optical module pcb high speed pcb layout An optical module PCB is a typical high-frequency, high-density HDI PCB precision board. Its material selection is closely related to transmission rate, link length, loss budget, and device platforms. While 10G and lower modules can use materials like high-Tg FR-4, high-speed modules operating at 25G, 56G, 100G, 400G, and 800G impose stringent requirements on low-loss materials, impedance control, and manufacturing consistency. Below are seven core layout design points and key differences compared to standard PCBs, focusing on high speed pcb layout and practical signal integrity engineering without rigid design fallacies. 1. Substrate Selection and StackUp Design Substrate selection and layer stackup form the foundation for stable high-frequency transmission, directly determining link insertion loss, impedance accuracy, and signal integrity. Multi-Dimensional Rate-Matched Selection: For 25G+ channels, select substrates considering Nyquist frequency, link length, insertion loss budget, dielectric loss, copper foil roughness, and stackup. For long-distance or low-loss channels, choose mid-to-low loss high-speed substrates. Non-critical areas like low-speed control and power can use high-Tg FR-4 to balance performance and cost on an optical module PCB. Adjacent Reference Ground Planes: High-speed differential signal layers should adopt a "signal-reference ground" structure to minimize edge-field coupling. Power layers should pair with adjacent ground layers to optimize PDN impedance via inter-layer capacitance. Pre-Simulation Impedance Modeling: Determine stackup parameters early through SI simulation. The industry standard target is typically 100 ohms differential impedance, with high-performance channels strictly controlling tolerances within +/- 5%. 2. High-Speed Differential TX/RX Signal Integrity High-speed differential signals are the core of data transmission in an optical module PCB. Design should focus on eliminating geometric discontinuities and parasitic interference. Symmetry and Equal Length: Match trace widths, spacing, bends, and via layouts for differential pairs. Advanced HDI pcb design requires controlling intra-pair length skew to prevent differential-to-common mode noise conversion. Trace Geometry Continuity: Use 45-degree angles or smooth arc transitions instead of rigid 90-degree turns. High-frequency reflections stem mostly from vias, pads, stubs, and split reference planes rather than standard trace corners. Minimal Via Structures and Stub Optimization: Minimize layer transitions. For long through-hole structures, apply back-drilling to remove residual stubs, cutting down reflections and resonances. （Backdrill + Via Stub） Unbroken High-Frequency Return Paths: Avoid routing differential traces across ground splits or slot gaps. Provide nearby stitching ground vias whenever signals switch layers. (Differential Pair + Reference Plane + Return Path) Crosstalk Mitigation: Apply the 3W rule during initial layout for proper spacing. For 112G PAM4 ultra-high-speed scenarios, refine trace spacing with 3D EM simulation and add ground via shielding walls where necessary. 3. Optoelectronic Isolation and Sensitive Layout Optical modules combine sensitive analog signals with high-speed digital logic. The analog front-end requires isolation from power and digital noise. Physical Isolation: Separate TOSA/ROSA components and TIA analog circuits from high-speed digital traces and switching power supplies based on form factors (SFP, QSFP, OSFP). Short Analog Traces: Keep weak analog traces from optical devices to TIA and driver ICs as short as possible, avoiding parallel routing alongside high-speed digital lines. Analog Circuit Shielding: Implement localized ground shielding or small metal shields around laser drivers and TIA circuits to isolate high-frequency digital noise. 4. Power Integrity (PI) Optimization Focus on low-impedance return paths, minimal current loops, and sub-region noise reduction. Minimal Loop Decoupling: Configure decoupling networks based on target PDN impedance. Place capacitors close to power pins to minimize parasitic inductance. Solid Ground Plane Priority: Maintain a continuous, low-impedance ground plane across the HDI PCB to provide a solid reference. Apply localized filtering for sensitive analog zones rather than single-point star grounding across the board. Thermal Copper Pour for Power Chips: Place large copper areas with thermal via arrays beneath heat-generating components like laser drivers to disperse heat quickly. 5. Thermal Management in HDI PCB Design Optical module DSPs, optical drivers, and laser diodes generate concentrated heat. High temperatures cause device aging, DK/Df parameter drift, and impedance shifts. Efficient Thermal Paths: Place dense thermal via arrays under high-power devices (DSP, TOSA) to transfer heat from the optical module PCB inner layers to the metal housing. Hot/Cold Component Partitioning: Isolate heat sources from temperature-sensitive optical and clock components to prevent thermal drift and premature aging. Symmetrical Design against Warpage: Balance copper distribution and layer stack-ups across the HDI PCB to manage thermal-mechanical stress during reflow soldering. （Thermal Path IC → Thermal Via → Copper Plane → Housing） 6. EMC and Grounding for High Speed PCB Layout Symmetrical Routing for Common-Mode Noise: Maintain structural symmetry in high-speed differential traces to reduce EMI radiation. Connect the module metal shell to the PCB ground for low-impedance shielding. Interface ESD Protection : Place TVS diodes and common-mode chokes near edge connectors to route ESD currents quickly to chassis ground. Isolate Interference Sources: Keep power inductors and switching regulators away from sensitive RX analog inputs to prevent magnetic coupling. 7. DFM Guidelines for Optical Module PCB Manufacturing Precise HDI pcb design and assembly standards ensure manufacturing yield for dense components. Precision Soldering Design: Use Via-in-Pad or micro-vias for high-density BGAs. For QFN thermal pads, use segmented stencil openings to reduce solder voiding and floating. Optical Alignment Tolerance: Match mechanical outline and mounting hole tolerances precisely with metal housings to avoid optical misalignments. Test Points and Gold Fingers: Keep test points off high-speed trunk lines. Use hard gold plating for edge connector gold fingers to ensure durability across insertion cycles. 8.Optical Module PCB vs Standard PCB Core Differences Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide by: Mila Sep 08,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hardware design type c design usb design usb type c design usb pcb design One of the most common pitfalls in Hardware Design for Type-C interfaces is confusing the legacy protocols used by USB-A ports with the native USB Type-C protocol. Some designers mistakenly treat D+ / D− as the core charging detection pins of Type-C, which can lead to design failures. The voltage is a normal 5V, the polarity is correct, but the device still does not charge, fails to be recognized, only works in one plug orientation, or has limited charging current. Compatibility issues may also occur with some phones. In many cases, there is basically one reason: CC1 and CC2 are not connected correctly. Let's look at the most common 5V Type-C charging configuration. Once you understand it, you can use it directly in your Type C Design. 1. The Most Important Conclusion For a Type-C interface, CC1 / CC2 are the core channels for power role detection, connection detection, current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ and D− do not handle basic Type-C power detection or USB PD negotiation in a standard C-to-C connection. This is one of the key differences between traditional USB and modern USB Type C Design: CC pins: The dedicated Type-C configuration channel used for power role detection, connection detection, plug orientation detection, Type-C current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ / D− pins: Mainly used for USB 2.0 data transmission and compatibility with certain legacy charging protocols, such as BC1.2. In simple terms: C-to-C charging: Basic power detection mainly relies on CC, not D+ / D−. A-to-C charging: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may use D+ / D− for charging detection. 2. Why Does C-to-C Charging Mainly Rely on CC? Taking a standard USB-C-to-USB-C charging connection as an example, the Source and Sink first establish a connection through the CC pins. The basic process is: 1. The charger provides Rp pull-ups on CC1 and CC2. 2. The phone or other powered device uses Rd pull-downs to indicate that it is a Sink. 3. The two sides detect the connection and determine the available Type-C current capability through CC. 4. If both sides support USB PD, they can further communicate through the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. It is important to note that 56KΩ, 22KΩ, and 10KΩ Rp values correspond to different advertised current capabilities. They should not be interpreted as “56KΩ directly unlocks 5V/3A.” Therefore, Type-C current capability detection and USB PD fast charging should be distinguished: Type-C current capability detection → Rp / Rd USB PD power negotiation → PD communication over CC D+ / D− mainly handle USB 2.0 data and certain legacy charging protocols. 3. CC vs. D+ / D−: What Does Each One Actually Do? CC1 / CC2: The Core Type-C Power and Connection Pins CC stands for Configuration Channel and is an important feature that distinguishes USB Type-C from traditional USB-A interfaces. CC1 and CC2 are mainly responsible for: Power role detection: Rp indicates a Source, while Rd indicates a Sink. Connection detection: Determines whether a valid connection has been established. Plug orientation detection: The active CC pin helps determine the plug orientation. Type-C current capability detection: The Source uses Rp to advertise its power capability. USB PD communication: USB PD devices use the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. Therefore, in a standard Type-C C-to-C power connection: Correct CC configuration is critical to proper device detection and power delivery. This is why CC routing and component placement are important in USB PCB Design. D+ / D−: Data Transmission and Legacy Charging Compatibility D+ / D− are essentially USB 2.0 differential data lines. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−. The key distinction is: C-to-C architecture: Basic Type-C power detection relies on CC. A-to-C architecture: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may involve D+ / D−. Therefore, the fact that D+ / D− were widely used for charging detection in the USB-A era does not mean that they are required for basic charging in a USB-C-to-USB-C connection. This distinction is important in practical USB Design . 4. Three Common CC Configurations + Applicable Scenarios The most common Type-C CC configurations can be divided into three categories: Sink, Source, and DRP. Typical resistor values include: Rp = 56KΩ / 22KΩ / 10KΩ Rd = 5.1KΩ The exact configuration depends on the device role and the Type-C / USB PD requirements. Configuration 1: Dual 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → 5.1KΩ → GND CC2 → 5.1KΩ → GND Applicable to: Phones, development boards, microcontroller boards, small appliances, and other Type-C devices that work as Sink devices. Function: The device indicates that it is a powered device, allowing the Source to detect the connection and determine the plug orientation. For basic Type-C power, this configuration can support standard 5V operation. Note: Two 5.1KΩ resistors do not automatically give the device USB PD fast-charging capability. If the device needs 9V, 12V, 15V, 20V, or other USB PD voltages, an appropriate USB PD Controller and supporting power-management circuitry are normally required. （Pull-Down Resistors） Configuration 2: Dual Rp Pull-Up Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → Rp → VBUS CC2 → Rp → VBUS Applicable to: Standard USB Type-C chargers, power banks with Type-C output ports, and other devices that work as a Source. Function: The Source uses CC to advertise its power capability so that the connected Type-C device can identify the power source. Different Rp configurations correspond to different Type-C default current capabilities. If USB PD fast charging is required, the design needs to support PD communication through the CC channel rather than relying on Rp alone. If compatibility with legacy USB-A charging protocols is also required, additional D+ / D− charging-detection circuitry or a charging protocol IC can be added according to the product requirements. （Pull-Up Resistors） Configuration 3: Dynamic Rp / Rd Switching for DRP Applicable to: Expansion docks, power banks, portable energy-storage devices, and other Type-C devices that need to dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles. Function: The device can determine its role according to the connected device and connection state, allowing it to operate as either a power source or a powered device. Note: DRP does not simply mean connecting Rp and Rd to CC1 / CC2 at the same time. In practical designs, a Type-C Controller or USB PD Controller is typically used to dynamically manage Rp / Rd, together with power-path control for safe bidirectional power delivery. （Rp / Rd Switching Resistors） Configuration 4: Type-C + USB PD Controller for Fast Charging If the product needs more than basic 5V power, such as: 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V or needs: Voltage, current, and power negotiation then Rp / Rd resistors alone are not sufficient. A typical architecture is: CC1 / CC2 → USB PD Controller → Power Path / DC-DC The PD Controller communicates through the CC channel and controls the downstream power circuitry according to the negotiated power profile. For USB Type C Design , this distinction is important when moving from basic 5V charging to USB PD fast charging. 5. A Common Mistake: Do Not Simply Short CC1 and CC2 Together Some Type-C designs try to make the interface work in both orientations by simply connecting: CC1 + CC2 → Shorted → One Rp or Rd. This should not be treated as a standard Type-C CC configuration. Simply shorting CC1 and CC2 can cause problems with proper connection detection and orientation handling, and may lead to compatibility issues in some applications. This is especially important for designs involving USB PD, higher current levels, or E-Marker cables. The correct approach is to configure the CC pins according to the required device role: Sink: CC1 → Rd CC2 → Rd Source: CC1 → Rp CC2 → Rp DRP: CC1 / CC2 → Type-C / PD Controller for dynamic role management Therefore, in USB PCB Design, CC1 and CC2 should be treated as separate configuration paths rather than simply tying them together. （CC1 and CC2 are shorted） 6. Final Takeaway: Check CC Before D+ / D− If you are designing a basic Type-C 5V Sink interface, the first thing to remember is simple: CC1 and CC2 each use a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor to GND. For a Type-C Source, select the appropriate Rp configuration according to the required power capability. If the product requires: Bidirectional charging → DRP 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V → USB PD Higher-current applications → Consider USB PD, cable capability, E-Marker requirements, and the complete power path D+ / D− should be determined separately according to whether the product needs: USB 2.0 data transmissionOr Legacy USB-A charging protocol compatibility. The biggest pitfall in Type-C Hardware Design is not simply whether VBUS measures 5V. The key is whether the interface correctly follows the USB Type-C rules for CC1 / CC2, Rp, Rd, DRP, and USB PD. Once these concepts are clear, basic Type-C charging interfaces become much easier to design correctly. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. If USB PD fast charging is required, the design needs to support PD communication through the CC channel rather than relying on Rp alone. If compatibility with legacy USB-A charging protocols is also required, additional D+ / D− charging-detection circuitry or a charging protocol IC can be added according to the product requirements. （Pull-Up Resistors） Configuration 3: Dynamic Rp / Rd Switching for DRP Applicable to: Expansion docks, power banks, portable energy-storage devices, and other Type-C devices that need to dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles. Function: The device can determine its role according to the connected device and connection state, allowing it to operate as either a power source or a powered device. Note: DRP does not simply mean connecting Rp and Rd to CC1 / CC2 at the same time. In practical designs, a Type-C Controller or USB PD Controller is typically used to dynamically manage Rp / Rd, together with power-path control for safe bidirectional power delivery. （Rp / Rd Switching Resistors） Configuration 4: Type-C + USB PD Controller for Fast Charging If the product needs more than basic 5V power, such as: 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V or needs: Voltage, current, and power negotiation then Rp / Rd resistors alone are not sufficient. A typical architecture is: CC1 / CC2 → USB PD Controller → Power Path / DC-DC The PD Controller communicates through the CC channel and controls the downstream power circuitry according to the negotiated power profile. For USB Type C Design , this distinction is important when moving from basic 5V charging to USB PD fast charging. 5. A Common Mistake: Do Not Simply Short CC1 and CC2 Together Some Type-C designs try to make the interface work in both orientations by simply connecting: CC1 + CC2 → Shorted → One Rp or Rd. This should not be treated as a standard Type-C CC configuration. Simply shorting CC1 and CC2 can cause problems with proper connection detection and orientation handling, and may lead to compatibility issues in some applications. This is especially important for designs involving USB PD, higher current levels, or E-Marker cables. The correct approach is to configure the CC pins according to the required device role: Sink: CC1 → Rd CC2 → Rd Source: CC1 → Rp CC2 → Rp DRP: CC1 / CC2 → Type-C / PD Controller for dynamic role management Therefore, in USB PCB Design, CC1 and CC2 should be treated as separate configuration paths rather than simply tying them together. （CC1 and CC2 are shorted） 6. Final Takeaway: Check CC Before D+ / D− If you are designing a basic Type-C 5V Sink interface, the first thing to remember is simple: CC1 and CC2 each use a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor to GND. For a Type-C Source, select the appropriate Rp configuration according to the required power capability. If the product requires: Bidirectional charging → DRP 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V → USB PD Higher-current applications → Consider USB PD, cable capability, E-Marker requirements, and the complete power path D+ / D− should be determined separately according to whether the product needs: USB 2.0 data transmissionOr Legacy USB-A charging protocol compatibility. The biggest pitfall in Type-C Hardware Design is not simply whether VBUS measures 5V. The key is whether the interface correctly follows the USB Type-C rules for CC1 / CC2, Rp, Rd, DRP, and USB PD. Once these concepts are clear, basic Type-C charging interfaces become much easier to design correctly. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCB Impedance Control Guide: How to Fix Impedance Discontinuities in PCB Layout PCB Impedance Control Guide: How to Fix Impedance Discontinuities in PCB Layout by: Mila Aug 31,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout impedance control pcb design pcb layout pcb impedance control In modern pcb design, maintaining signal integrity relies on a stable transmission path. Proper impedance control prevents signal reflection and ensures stable performance across your board. This article explores why pcb impedance control is essential, where discontinuities typically occur during pcb layout, and how targeted optimizations improve overall channel quality. 1. Why Impedance Control Matters Why do we need pcb impedance control, how do we achieve it, and which aspects require adjustments? The simulation results below tell the story—showing schematics with and without impedance matching. When impedance mismatch occurs across a transmission link, signals reflect at points of impedance discontinuity. These reflected signals combine with original signals, resulting in waveform anomalies like overshoot, undershoot, ringing, and glitches. Heavy reflection can cause false sampling at the receiver, compromising high-speed system stability. Effective impedance control requires precise stackup planning. Before routing your high-speed signals, make sure to test your trace impedance with our free online calculator to determine the exact trace width and spacing needed. 2. Key Areas for Impedance Optimization From the IC package interior to PCB traces and receiver ICs, high-speed links contain multiple regions vulnerable to impedance mismatch. Common risk areas include: IC package pads BGA breakout routing Layer-change vias Termination resistors, capacitors, and connector pads Differential pair length matching Discontinuous return paths Discontinuous reference planes Stubs and branch trace routing Impedance discontinuities often occur near IC package pads. While design space here is limited, keeping thin traces short and adding ground cutouts (anti-pads) under adjacent layers can slightly raise impedance—a approach often seen in PCIe Gen5 design guidelines. Impedance shifts also happen after signal lines exit the IC through capacitors, resistors, vias, and connectors. TDR data clearly demonstrates the difference before and after optimization. During length matching, inevitable small serpentines on differential pairs can trigger local impedance disruptions. Length compensation segments should be placed in areas with controlled impedance environments, continuous reference planes, and safe distances from sensitive structures like vias or pads. For regions with structural discontinuities, combine topology planning with SI simulation for co-optimization rather than blindly adding serpentine traces along continuous mainlines. Disrupted return paths cause impedance drops and ground bounce. When high-speed signals change layers without nearby ground stitching vias, returning current is forced to detour. This increases loop area, parasitic inductance, electromagnetic field shifts, crosstalk, EMI risks, and impedance mismatch. The diagram below shows an impedance jump caused by a reference plane discontinuity. When traces cross reference plane splits, slots, or other discontinuous regions, the original return path is disrupted. This alters the local transmission line structure, creating impedance mismatch and additional signal integrity risks during pcb layout . The diagram below shows an impedance jump caused by a stub. 3. Benefits of Impedance Optimization The points mentioned above are mostly locations where impedance discontinuities occur along the link. Below is a data comparison of an entire high-speed differential transmission line before and after optimization. The link includes various impedance discontinuity points, such as IC pin output pads, layer-change vias, capacitors, load-end connectors, and stubs. By optimizing discontinuous impedance structures within the link—including pads, vias, passive components, connectors, and stubs—local signal reflections are reduced, and the channel's return loss performance is significantly improved. In this case, after the impedance structures were optimized, the channel's insertion loss also improved, demonstrating that mitigating severe structural discontinuities helps enhance the overall performance of high-speed channels in pcb design. 4. Practical Optimization Methods Proper pcb design requires systematic approaches across different elements. The following sections outline practical optimization workflows for passive components (based on 4-layer 1.6mm stackups), vias, and length-matching techniques essential for modern pcb layout: (Note: The following optimization case uses a 4-layer, 1.6 mm total thickness PCB as an example. Actual impedance cannot be determined solely by total board thickness; it must be calculated and verified using dielectric thickness, copper thickness, material Dk, trace width/spacing, and target impedance.) Verify Now Blog > Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design power module ir drop remote sens Many DC-DC power chips provide a Remote-Sense function. However, many designers mistake it for an optional secondary connection and wire it directly near the power module's local output. This setup effectively renders remote sampling useless. During the debugging phase, various anomalies may occur: while the local output voltage of the power module appears normal, the supply voltage at the BGA core experiences continuous droop; the power supply may exhibit audible noise, Loop Stability degradation, and severe output voltage ripple fluctuations. Remote-Sense is not a redundant line, but a Kelvin Sensing line used to measure the actual voltage at the load. The main power path carries high load currents, whereas the Force & Sense architecture ensures the Force & Sense signal paths remain isolated. Because the Force & Sense sensing line features high input impedance with minimal input bias current, it avoids the significant voltage drops present along the power delivery path, thereby measuring the load voltage more accurately. 1. Root Cause of Remote-Sense Application: DC IR Drop Modern processor core supply voltages continue to drop, with typical values around 0.8V or 0.85V, while operating currents can reach tens to hundreds of amperes. Even with wide copper traces and dense via arrays on the PCB, inherent DC resistance remains in the copper foil, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout regions along the power path. As large load currents pass through these impedances, a noticeable IR Drop occurs. For example, assume a DC-DC module has a local output voltage of 1.0V, and the total equivalent resistance of the power path from the module to an FPGA's BGA power pins is 1.5mΩ. Under a 100A load current, the voltage drop VIR Drop = I × R = 100A × 1.5mΩ = 150mV. Thus, while the local output stays at 1.0V, the actual voltage at the FPGA BGA pins drops to approximately 0.85V due to IR Drop along the copper, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout. If the sampling point is placed locally at the DC-DC output, the Feedback Loop can only detect the local 1.0V rail. The Feedback Loop remains unaware of the 0.15V lost before reaching the load. For low-voltage core supplies, the allowable voltage tolerance is tight, depending on processor, FPGA, or ASIC specifications. Such voltage degradation caused by IR Drop leads to full-load crashes, frequency throttling, and inadequate timing margins on high-speed interfaces. Remote-Sense resolves this problem: by routing the Remote-Sense sampling line directly near the load chip's power pins, the system detects the true voltage at the load. When the detected load voltage falls below the target, the Feedback Loop increases the power stage output to compensate for the IR Drop along the power delivery path. (Remote-Sense Working Principle) 2. Kelvin Remote Voltage Sensing: Force & Sense At its core, Remote-Sense relies on Kelvin Sensing principles to segregate the high-current power path from the voltage detection line. Force Power Path The power path delivers actual energy to the load and requires sufficient copper width, copper weight, and parallel vias to lower impedance. Because this pathway carries the full load current, it inevitably suffers from IR Drop. Sense Sampling Path The Force & Sense sensing line has high impedance and carries only a tiny input bias current. According to V = I × R, because the current flowing through the Force & Sense sensing line is negligible, its trace resistance creates virtually no voltage drop compared to the high-current power line. Consequently, Kelvin Sensing measures the electrical potential at the load with high accuracy. The power converter's internal Feedback Loop continuously measures the error between the sense voltage and an internal reference voltage, adjusting power delivery to compensate for PCB power losses. For ICs featuring Differential Sensing, both VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be fully connected as specified in the datasheet. Incorrectly connecting only a single sense line may cause reference errors or disable remote sampling altogether. （Kelvin Force/Sense Schematic ） 3. Remote-Sense PCB Layout Guidelines Remote-Sense is far more than a simple jumper trace. Sampling point placement, routing methods, Noise Isolation, filtering, and Multi-Load Topology configurations all impose strict constraints. Improper implementation fails to compensate for IR Drop and risks introducing high-frequency noise into the Feedback Loop, inducing output fluctuations, degraded Loop Stability, or audible squealing. VSENSE+ / VSENSE- Differential Pair Routing VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be routed using Differential Pair Routing, kept closely coupled in identical environments. Avoid placing either trace near SW Nodes, clock lines, or other noisy sources, and never run them parallel to power switching nodes over long distances. Adequate Noise Isolation is essential to prevent interference. If the two traces experience different distances to noise sources, varying Ground Plane Reference structures, or unequal surrounding copper, external interference couples unevenly into the lines. This asymmetry converts into differential-mode noise, directly corrupting the Feedback Loop. Therefore, the main objective of Differential Pair Routing is not simply maximizing line width, but ensuring both lines share a symmetrical, low-noise environment with effective Noise Isolation, minimal loop area, and a solid Ground Plane Reference. Sensing Point Placement Incorrect: Placing the Sensing Point Placement directly across the DC-DC module's local output capacitors. This neutralizes the benefits of Remote-Sense, as the controller senses only the local output while uncompensated losses persist down the line. Correct: Proper Sensing Point Placement requires connecting the lines as close as possible to the load chip's actual power pins (e.g., near the BGA power pins), adhering to the manufacturer's recommended Sensing Point Placement guidelines. Input filtering and Decoupling Capacitors must be placed as close to the chip power pins as possible to lower the high-frequency current loop impedance at the load. The core principle of Remote-Sense layout is: The sense point must represent the true voltage received by the load, not an intermediate node along the power path. Never place sense points arbitrarily along intermediate nodes or directly on power copper pour for layout convenience. Even if schematics correctly define Differential Sensing, improper Sensing Point Placement on the PCB invalidates the feature. （Remote-Sense PCB Layout） Controller-Side RC Low-Pass Filter Sense traces often traverse long PCB paths, making them vulnerable to high-frequency interference from switching SW Nodes, DDR buses, clocks, and high-speed traces. Proper Noise Isolation helps, but if high-frequency noise reaches the sensing node, it induces output jitter and degrades Loop Stability. For long sense traces or noisy environments, place an RC Low-Pass Filter near the sense pins according to datasheet recommendations to suppress coupled switching noise. Some IC manufacturers recommend an RC Low-Pass Filter consisting of tens of ohms in series and nanofarad-range capacitors. However, specific R and C parameters must strictly follow vendor datasheets and be validated through Loop Stability testing rather than using generic values. Note that an RC Low-Pass Filter introduces an additional time constant, requiring evaluation regarding its impact on loop bandwidth, Transient Response, and overall stability. Multi-Load Topology: Reference Point at Key Load When a single power rail supplies multiple BGA devices, a Multi-Load Topology must not place the sense point at a random common node or simply at the load closest to the converter. In a Multi-Load Topology, evaluate system voltage tolerances, load currents, and power path drops to position the reference point at the most voltage-sensitive load experiencing the highest drop. For example, in a chain of DC-DC -> Load A -> Load B -> Load C, if Load C has the tightest tolerance and highest line drop in this Multi-Load Topology, connect the sense reference point directly to Load C's supply pins. This ensures the loop prioritizes the voltage margin of the critical load, while closer loads are powered via the main power path without serving as feedback references. Handling Unused Remote-Sense Pins If a design does not enable Remote-Sense, do not leave the VSENSE+ and VSENSE- pins floating, as a Floating Pin Hazard will disrupt feedback control. For controllers relying on external sense inputs, a Floating Pin Hazard leaves input potentials uncontrolled, causing abnormal output voltages and potential device damage. To avoid a Floating Pin Hazard, consult the datasheet. Devices supporting local sense mode typically require connecting VSENSE+ to local VOUT+ and VSENSE- to local GND. Always follow the manufacturer's specified wiring for local sensing, as internal architectures vary. 4. Remote-Sense Cannot Replace Power Integrity / PDN Design Remote-Sense is not a substitute for proper load-side decoupling and low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN design. Remote-Sense primarily compensates for DC or low-frequency voltage losses along the power path. When a CPU, FPGA, GPU, or ASIC undergoes a fast step change, the Transient Response of the feedback loop cannot react instantaneously. During these events, Decoupling Capacitors and a low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN supply transient current and mitigate sharp voltage dips. Therefore, comprehensive Power Integrity / PDN design requires integrating multiple strategies: Low-impedance Power/GND planes with a continuous Ground Plane Reference Adequate copper width and parallel via arrays Load-side MLCC Decoupling Capacitors Bulk capacitors Optimized power routing Remote-Sense implementation High Transient Response and stable loop margins Remote-Sense, power path optimization, and Decoupling Capacitors complement each other rather than act as replacements. 5. Additional Remote-Sense Constraints and Safety Considerations If Remote-Sense is connected to a distant load without being properly configured or enabled, incorrect feedback compensation may drive the local voltage too high, triggering OVP / UVP Protection, instability, or exceeding maximum operating limits. Always consult the datasheet to confirm: Support for Remote-Sense and Differential Sensing Allowable voltage ranges for sense inputs Correct connections for local sensing mode Requirements for an RC Low-Pass Filter Optimal Sensing Point Placement Interaction between Remote-Sense and OVP / UVP Protection thresholds Maximum allowable sense trace lengths and routing layouts If the sense voltage drops excessively due to open circuits or extreme line losses, improperly configured controllers may trigger OVP / UVP Protection to prevent overvoltage damage at the local output or undervoltage failures at the load. Ultimately, Remote-Sense is not just about routing two lines to the load. It ensures the feedback loop accurately measures the actual voltage delivered to the load while maintaining reliable OVP / UVP Protection and preventing noise or parasitics from degrading system stability.l Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design power module ir drop remote sens Many DC-DC power chips provide a Remote-Sense function. However, many designers mistake it for an optional secondary connection and wire it directly near the power module's local output. This setup effectively renders remote sampling useless. During the debugging phase, various anomalies may occur: while the local output voltage of the power module appears normal, the supply voltage at the BGA core experiences continuous droop; the power supply may exhibit audible noise, Loop Stability degradation, and severe output voltage ripple fluctuations. Remote-Sense is not a redundant line, but a Kelvin Sensing line used to measure the actual voltage at the load. The main power path carries high load currents, whereas the Force & Sense architecture ensures the Force & Sense signal paths remain isolated. Because the Force & Sense sensing line features high input impedance with minimal input bias current, it avoids the significant voltage drops present along the power delivery path, thereby measuring the load voltage more accurately. 1. Root Cause of Remote-Sense Application: DC IR Drop Modern processor core supply voltages continue to drop, with typical values around 0.8V or 0.85V, while operating currents can reach tens to hundreds of amperes. Even with wide copper traces and dense via arrays on the PCB, inherent DC resistance remains in the copper foil, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout regions along the power path. As large load currents pass through these impedances, a noticeable IR Drop occurs. For example, assume a DC-DC module has a local output voltage of 1.0V, and the total equivalent resistance of the power path from the module to an FPGA's BGA power pins is 1.5mΩ. Under a 100A load current, the voltage drop VIR Drop = I × R = 100A × 1.5mΩ = 150mV. Thus, while the local output stays at 1.0V, the actual voltage at the FPGA BGA pins drops to approximately 0.85V due to IR Drop along the copper, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout. If the sampling point is placed locally at the DC-DC output, the Feedback Loop can only detect the local 1.0V rail. The Feedback Loop remains unaware of the 0.15V lost before reaching the load. For low-voltage core supplies, the allowable voltage tolerance is tight, depending on processor, FPGA, or ASIC specifications. Such voltage degradation caused by IR Drop leads to full-load crashes, frequency throttling, and inadequate timing margins on high-speed interfaces. Remote-Sense resolves this problem: by routing the Remote-Sense sampling line directly near the load chip's power pins, the system detects the true voltage at the load. When the detected load voltage falls below the target, the Feedback Loop increases the power stage output to compensate for the IR Drop along the power delivery path. (Remote-Sense Working Principle) 2. Kelvin Remote Voltage Sensing: Force & Sense At its core, Remote-Sense relies on Kelvin Sensing principles to segregate the high-current power path from the voltage detection line. Force Power Path The power path delivers actual energy to the load and requires sufficient copper width, copper weight, and parallel vias to lower impedance. Because this pathway carries the full load current, it inevitably suffers from IR Drop. Sense Sampling Path The Force & Sense sensing line has high impedance and carries only a tiny input bias current. According to V = I × R, because the current flowing through the Force & Sense sensing line is negligible, its trace resistance creates virtually no voltage drop compared to the high-current power line. Consequently, Kelvin Sensing measures the electrical potential at the load with high accuracy. The power converter's internal Feedback Loop continuously measures the error between the sense voltage and an internal reference voltage, adjusting power delivery to compensate for PCB power losses. For ICs featuring Differential Sensing, both VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be fully connected as specified in the datasheet. Incorrectly connecting only a single sense line may cause reference errors or disable remote sampling altogether. （Kelvin Force/Sense Schematic ） 3. Remote-Sense PCB Layout Guidelines Remote-Sense is far more than a simple jumper trace. Sampling point placement, routing methods, Noise Isolation, filtering, and Multi-Load Topology configurations all impose strict constraints. Improper implementation fails to compensate for IR Drop and risks introducing high-frequency noise into the Feedback Loop, inducing output fluctuations, degraded Loop Stability, or audible squealing. VSENSE+ / VSENSE- Differential Pair Routing VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be routed using Differential Pair Routing, kept closely coupled in identical environments. Avoid placing either trace near SW Nodes, clock lines, or other noisy sources, and never run them parallel to power switching nodes over long distances. Adequate Noise Isolation is essential to prevent interference. If the two traces experience different distances to noise sources, varying Ground Plane Reference structures, or unequal surrounding copper, external interference couples unevenly into the lines. This asymmetry converts into differential-mode noise, directly corrupting the Feedback Loop. Therefore, the main objective of Differential Pair Routing is not simply maximizing line width, but ensuring both lines share a symmetrical, low-noise environment with effective Noise Isolation, minimal loop area, and a solid Ground Plane Reference. Sensing Point Placement Incorrect: Placing the Sensing Point Placement directly across the DC-DC module's local output capacitors. This neutralizes the benefits of Remote-Sense, as the controller senses only the local output while uncompensated losses persist down the line. Correct: Proper Sensing Point Placement requires connecting the lines as close as possible to the load chip's actual power pins (e.g., near the BGA power pins), adhering to the manufacturer's recommended Sensing Point Placement guidelines. Input filtering and Decoupling Capacitors must be placed as close to the chip power pins as possible to lower the high-frequency current loop impedance at the load. The core principle of Remote-Sense layout is: The sense point must represent the true voltage received by the load, not an intermediate node along the power path. Never place sense points arbitrarily along intermediate nodes or directly on power copper pour for layout convenience. Even if schematics correctly define Differential Sensing, improper Sensing Point Placement on the PCB invalidates the feature. （Remote-Sense PCB Layout） Controller-Side RC Low-Pass Filter Sense traces often traverse long PCB paths, making them vulnerable to high-frequency interference from switching SW Nodes, DDR buses, clocks, and high-speed traces. Proper Noise Isolation helps, but if high-frequency noise reaches the sensing node, it induces output jitter and degrades Loop Stability. For long sense traces or noisy environments, place an RC Low-Pass Filter near the sense pins according to datasheet recommendations to suppress coupled switching noise. Some IC manufacturers recommend an RC Low-Pass Filter consisting of tens of ohms in series and nanofarad-range capacitors. However, specific R and C parameters must strictly follow vendor datasheets and be validated through Loop Stability testing rather than using generic values. Note that an RC Low-Pass Filter introduces an additional time constant, requiring evaluation regarding its impact on loop bandwidth, Transient Response, and overall stability. Multi-Load Topology: Reference Point at Key Load When a single power rail supplies multiple BGA devices, a Multi-Load Topology must not place the sense point at a random common node or simply at the load closest to the converter. In a Multi-Load Topology, evaluate system voltage tolerances, load currents, and power path drops to position the reference point at the most voltage-sensitive load experiencing the highest drop. For example, in a chain of DC-DC -> Load A -> Load B -> Load C, if Load C has the tightest tolerance and highest line drop in this Multi-Load Topology, connect the sense reference point directly to Load C's supply pins. This ensures the loop prioritizes the voltage margin of the critical load, while closer loads are powered via the main power path without serving as feedback references. Handling Unused Remote-Sense Pins If a design does not enable Remote-Sense, do not leave the VSENSE+ and VSENSE- pins floating, as a Floating Pin Hazard will disrupt feedback control. For controllers relying on external sense inputs, a Floating Pin Hazard leaves input potentials uncontrolled, causing abnormal output voltages and potential device damage. To avoid a Floating Pin Hazard, consult the datasheet. Devices supporting local sense mode typically require connecting VSENSE+ to local VOUT+ and VSENSE- to local GND. Always follow the manufacturer's specified wiring for local sensing, as internal architectures vary. 4. Remote-Sense Cannot Replace Power Integrity / PDN Design Remote-Sense is not a substitute for proper load-side decoupling and low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN design. Remote-Sense primarily compensates for DC or low-frequency voltage losses along the power path. When a CPU, FPGA, GPU, or ASIC undergoes a fast step change, the Transient Response of the feedback loop cannot react instantaneously. During these events, Decoupling Capacitors and a low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN supply transient current and mitigate sharp voltage dips. Therefore, comprehensive Power Integrity / PDN design requires integrating multiple strategies: Low-impedance Power/GND planes with a continuous Ground Plane Reference Adequate copper width and parallel via arrays Load-side MLCC Decoupling Capacitors Bulk capacitors Optimized power routing Remote-Sense implementation High Transient Response and stable loop margins Remote-Sense, power path optimization, and Decoupling Capacitors complement each other rather than act as replacements. 5. Additional Remote-Sense Constraints and Safety Considerations If Remote-Sense is connected to a distant load without being properly configured or enabled, incorrect feedback compensation may drive the local voltage too high, triggering OVP / UVP Protection, instability, or exceeding maximum operating limits. Always consult the datasheet to confirm: Support for Remote-Sense and Differential Sensing Allowable voltage ranges for sense inputs Correct connections for local sensing mode Requirements for an RC Low-Pass Filter Optimal Sensing Point Placement Interaction between Remote-Sense and OVP / UVP Protection thresholds Maximum allowable sense trace lengths and routing layouts If the sense voltage drops excessively due to open circuits or extreme line losses, improperly configured controllers may trigger OVP / UVP Protection to prevent overvoltage damage at the local output or undervoltage failures at the load. Ultimately, Remote-Sense is not just about routing two lines to the load. It ensures the feedback loop accurately measures the actual voltage delivered to the load while maintaining reliable OVP / UVP Protection and preventing noise or parasitics from degrading system stability.l Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
